opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of our early pivots came from one root cause: we started from a technology we loved, not from a customer problem we deeply understood.

Taichi began as a research project. I was a PhD student working on physical simulation and computer graphics, and I was frustrated by how hard it was to write high-performance code. You'd have a beautiful idea on the whiteboard, and then spend weeks fighting with CUDA, memory layouts, and sparse data structures. So we built a language to solve *our own* pain. And it worked. People in the research community liked it, the open-source project grew, and we got a lot of GitHub stars.

When we started the company, there was a natural temptation to assume that because developers liked the tool, there was obviously a business there. But stars aren't revenue, and enthusiasm from researchers doesn't automatically translate into someone with a budget who needs you to exist. So in the early days we tried several directions, different application areas and different ways of packaging the technology, and each time we learned something about who actually feels the pain strongly enough to pay for a solution.

Looking back, a few things were going on.

First, we were engineers and researchers, and we underestimated how different building a product is from building a great piece of technology. A compiler can be elegant and still not be a product. A product has to fit into someone's workflow, their organization, their purchasing process.

Second, the market was moving. Graphics, simulation, AI, digital content creation: these areas were changing quickly, and some assumptions we made at the start simply stopped being true a year or two later. Part of a pivot isn't that you were wrong; it's that the world changed and you have to respond.

Third, and this is the more personal part, I had to learn to separate my identity from the project. When you've spent years on something, every pivot feels like admitting failure. But I came to see it differently. A pivot is just updating your beliefs with new evidence. In research we do that all the time: an experiment fails, you adjust the hypothesis. Running a company should be no different. The mistake isn't pivoting; the mistake is pivoting too slowly because your ego is attached to the old plan.

So if I summarize: the pivots were the cost of starting technology-first, combined with a fast-changing environment and our own inexperience as founders. I don't regret them. I think they were tuition. The important thing is whether each one made us sharper about who we serve and why they should care. I'd say they did.

r001.rationale: The response says the company started with technology it loved instead of a deeply understood customer problem, then assumed the tool could be a business. It connects that customer and purpose gap to trying different directions and learning what customers would pay for.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think the pivots came down to one gap: I was very good at building technology, and I was not yet good at understanding why anyone would pay for it.

Taichi started as my PhD project at MIT. It was a compiler and a programming language for high-performance graphics and physics simulation. The research community loved it, we open-sourced it, it got tens of thousands of GitHub stars. So when we started the company in 2019, the natural assumption was: people love the tech, therefore there is a business here. That turned out to be a leap of logic rather than a fact.

The first lesson was that "open-source popularity" and "willingness to pay" are almost unrelated signals. Developers starred the repo because it was elegant and fun to use. But the people with budgets, in gaming, in robotics, in industrial simulation, did not wake up thinking "I need a better differentiable programming language." They had concrete problems, like "my cloth simulation is too slow for this shipping deadline." We kept trying to sell the general-purpose tool when they wanted a solved problem.

So we pivoted toward applications: real-time physics engines, then simulation for specific verticals. Each of those pivots taught us something about where the pain was real and where it was just intellectually interesting to us. Some directions had enthusiastic users but tiny markets. Some had big markets but we were not differentiated enough, because the customer did not care that our compiler was clever if the competitor's result looked the same on screen.

Looking back, I would say two things drove the pivots. One was simple ignorance about go-to-market, which you can only cure by getting out there and being wrong in front of customers. The other was ego, in a mild form: I wanted the world to value what I had built, rather than building what the world valued. Letting go of that took a while, and I think every technical founder has to go through it.

The reframe that eventually helped me was to treat the company itself like a research project. Each pivot is an experiment, you form a hypothesis about who the customer is, you test it as cheaply as possible, and you update honestly. Once I stopped seeing pivots as failures and started seeing them as data, the process became a lot less painful. Not fun exactly, but less painful.

r001.rationale: The response says the company assumed popular technology implied a business, then tried to sell a general-purpose tool when customers needed specific problems solved. It explicitly links not understanding why customers would pay to building the wrong thing.

astra-6.text:
I think the way to understand those early pivots is as a learning process. When you start a company, you have assumptions about what people need and where your technology can be useful. Then you talk to users and try to build something they actually want, and those assumptions get tested.

For me, the important distinction is between the goal and the path. You can stay committed to the goal while realizing that your first approach isn’t the right one. A pivot should reflect something you’ve learned—about the problem, the customer, or what you can deliver—not simply a desire to chase a new opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response describes testing assumptions and learning through users, but does not say the company failed to clarify why it was building something or that this caused it to build the wrong thing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an early pivot is usually a process of learning. You start with a hypothesis about what your technology can do and why people will want it. But those are two different questions. Something can be technically interesting without solving a problem that customers consider important enough to pay for.

So, to me, the key is to distinguish the long-term conviction from the initial approach. You can stay committed to the underlying opportunity while changing the product, the customer, or how you bring it to market. Changing direction isn’t necessarily a loss of conviction; it can mean you understand the problem better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from initial hypotheses and distinguishing technical interest from customer demand, but it does not state that the company failed to clarify why it was building something or that this caused it to build the wrong thing.
